headings.title: Introduction to Diarrhoeal Diseases in Children
headings.content: Diarrhoeal diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among infants and young children, particularly in low- and middle-income countries like Nigeria. Within the primary health care system, understanding the true burden and clinical impact of childhood diarrhoea is essential for reducing preventable deaths. Diarrhoea is broadly defined as the passage of three or more loose, watery, or liquid stools per day, or more frequently than is normal for the individual child. It disrupts normal physiological balance by causing rapid loss of water and vital electrolytes, which can precipitate life-threatening dehydration and shock within hours if left unmanaged. Nurses operating in community health centers and immunization clinics play a pivotal role in early identification, caregiver education, and immediate intervention. Because acute watery diarrhoea can lead to severe hypovolemic complications, recognizing the condition goes beyond simply counting stool frequency; it requires a holistic evaluation of the child's overall wellness, nutritional status, and environment. Healthcare providers must recognize that diarrhoea does not occur in a vacuum; it is deeply intertwined with poverty, inadequate sanitation, and poor hygiene practices. Consequently, tackling diarrhoeal diseases requires a dual approach of acute clinical management and aggressive preventive education targeted at mothers, caregivers, and community leaders. By mastering the epidemiological patterns and clinical manifestations of childhood diarrhoea, nursing students can effectively contribute to national and international child survival strategies and significantly lower under-five mortality rates.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Types of Diarrhoea
headings.content: To effectively manage diarrhoeal diseases, nursing students must understand the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms and the different types of diarrhoea. Diarrhoea is generally categorized into three main types based on duration and mechanism: acute watery diarrhoea, acute bloody diarrhoea (dysentery), and persistent diarrhoea. Acute watery diarrhoea lasts for several hours or days and poses the immediate risk of severe dehydration due to net fluid secretion in the intestines. Pathophysiologically, enteropathogens interact with the intestinal mucosa, altering transport mechanisms. Some pathogens produce enterotoxins that stimulate active secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen without causing structural damage, while others cause invasive damage leading to inflammation, ulceration, and blood in the stool, as seen in dysentery. Persistent diarrhoea is defined as an episode that lasts for 14 days or longer, often resulting in severe nutritional depletion, mucosal atrophy, and systemic complications. Understanding these mechanisms helps nurses differentiate between simple secretory fluid losses and invasive infections that may require targeted antimicrobial therapy alongside supportive rehydration. Furthermore, appreciating the duration categories guides the choice of nutritional interventions and referral criteria, ensuring that children receive comprehensive, mechanism-based care tailored to their specific clinical presentation.

headings.title: Common Causes and Risk Factors in Primary Health Care
headings.content: Childhood diarrhoea is predominantly infectious in etiology, driven by a range of viral, bacterial, and parasitic agents. Rotavirus is historically the leading cause of severe, dehydrating acute watery diarrhoea in infants globally. Other significant viral pathogens include enteric adenoviruses and noroviruses. Bacterial causes, such as Escherichia coli (particularly enterotoxigenic and enteroinvasive strains), Shigella species, Salmonella, and Vibrio cholerae, frequently contribute to both watery diarrhoea and dysenteric presentations. Parasitic infections like Giardia lamblia and Cryptosporidium are also notable, especially in cases of persistent diarrhoea among immunocompromised or malnourished children. In primary health care settings, identifying environmental and behavioral risk factors is just as crucial as knowing the pathogens. Major risk factors include the use of unsafe drinking water, poor personal and domestic hygiene (such as infrequent handwashing with soap), improper disposal of human waste and infant feces, lack of exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life, and living in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions. Malnutrition acts as both a risk factor and a consequence, creating a vicious cycle where a malnourished child has compromised gut immunity, making them more susceptible to severe infections that further worsen their nutritional status. Nursing interventions must therefore target these modifiable environmental and nutritional determinants during routine health education sessions.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Assessing Dehydration Status
headings.content: Clinical assessment of a child with diarrhoea focuses primarily on evaluating the child's hydration status to determine the appropriate treatment plan. Under the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, dehydration status is categorized into three clinical classes: No Dehydration, Some Dehydration, and Severe Dehydration. Nurses must systematically assess four key signs: general condition, eyes, skin pinch, and thirst. A child with no dehydration is alert, has normal eyes, drinks normally, and the skin pinch goes back immediately. A child with some dehydration may appear restless or irritable, have sunken eyes, drink eagerly and with thirst, and the skin pinch goes back slowly (between 2 and 2 seconds). A child with severe dehydration exhibits lethargy or unconsciousness, very sunken and dry eyes, drinks poorly or is unable to drink, and the skin pinch goes back very slowly (longer than 2 seconds). Additional clinical assessments must include checking for fever, examining the stool for blood, measuring nutritional status (such as assessing for severe acute malnutrition using mid-upper arm circumference or weight-for-height), and evaluating the frequency and duration of vomiting and diarrhoea. Accurate assessment prevents both under-treatment of critical fluid losses and over-treatment with aggressive intravenous therapies, ensuring that children receive the precise level of care required for recovery.

headings.title: Management Using Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) and Zinc Supplementation
headings.content: The cornerstone of managing acute diarrhoea without severe dehydration is Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT), utilizing low-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution. Low-osmolarity ORS contains reduced amounts of glucose and sodium, which significantly decreases stool output, vomiting, and the need for unscheduled intravenous infusions. Nurses must educate caregivers on how to correctly mix a packet of ORS in clean water and administer it frequently using a cup and spoon rather than a feeding bottle, which can introduce bacteria. In addition to ORS, zinc supplementation is a vital therapeutic intervention recommended by the World Health Organization for all children with diarrhoea. Zinc should be administered daily for 10 to 14 days (20 mg per day for children over six months, and 10 mg per day for infants under six months). Zinc supplementation significantly reduces the duration and severity of the current diarrhoeal episode and also decreases the likelihood of new episodes occurring in the subsequent two to three months by restoring intestinal mucosal integrity, supporting immune function, and enhancing brush border enzyme activity. Nurses must demonstrate proper administration, explain potential side effects such as mild metallic taste or temporary nausea, and emphasize the importance of completing the full 14-day course even after symptoms have resolved.

headings.title: Nutritional Care and Continued Feeding During and After Diarrhoea
headings.content: Nutritional management is an integral component of diarrhoeal care, moving away from the outdated practice of 'resting the bowel' through fasting. Continuing feeding during and immediately after a diarrhoeal episode prevents nutritional deterioration, preserves intestinal mucosal function, and speeds up recovery. Breastfed infants should continue to be breastfed on demand and more frequently, as breast milk is easily digestible and provides essential immunological protection. For older children who have started complementary foods, caregivers should offer frequent, small meals containing nutrient-dense, locally available foods rich in energy and micronutrients, such as mashed porridges with added oils, pulses, and lean meats. During convalescence, an extra meal per day should be given for at least two weeks to help the child catch up on lost weight and nutrients. Nurses must actively counsel mothers to overcome cultural food taboos that often restrict feeding during illness. If the child experiences persistent diarrhoea, dietary modifications may be necessary, but food restriction should be avoided unless medically indicated for specific intolerances. Proper nutritional counseling empowers caregivers to support active recovery and prevent long-term growth faltering and malnutrition.

headings.title: Indications for Intravenous Fluid Therapy and Hospital Referral
headings.content: While most children with diarrhoea can be successfully managed outpatient with ORS and zinc, certain clinical presentations require immediate intravenous (IV) fluid therapy and urgent hospital referral. Intravenous fluids (such as Ringer's Lactate solution) are indicated for children assessed with severe dehydration who are lethargic, unconscious, or unable to drink, or when oral rehydration fails due to persistent, profuse vomiting. In primary health care clinics where IV access cannot be established or where complications such as severe acute malnutrition, suspected cholera, systemic sepsis, or bloody dysentery with high fever are present, emergency referral to a higher-level facility is mandatory. During pre-referral transport, nurses must initiate treatment by giving ORS if the child can still drink, or start a nasogastric tube rehydration if IV access is unavailable, provided the child is not severely lethargic. Nurses must accompany the referral note with clear documentation of the child's fluid intake, assessment findings, and treatments already administered. Recognizing danger signs and facilitating prompt hospital transfer saves children from irreversible hypovolemic shock, renal failure, and death.

headings.title: Prevention Strategies and Community Health Education
headings.content: Prevention is the most sustainable and cost-effective approach to controlling diarrhoeal diseases in communities. Comprehensive prevention strategies focus on five key pillars: promotion of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, improved access to safe drinking water, proper sanitation and hygienic waste disposal, handwashing with soap at critical times, and scaling up rotavirus vaccination. Community health nurses play a vital role in organizing health education campaigns, conducting mother-support group meetings, and demonstrating proper handwashing techniques in schools and market places. Safe water management involves treating household water through boiling, chlorination, or filtration. Sanitation efforts require promoting the construction and proper use of latrines and ensuring safe disposal of infant feces, which are often more infectious than adult stools. Furthermore, advocating for and administering rotavirus vaccines through routine immunization schedules drastically reduces the incidence of severe viral gastroenteritis among vulnerable populations. Through persistent community outreach and empowering local stakeholders, nurses help dismantle the environmental and behavioral bottlenecks that sustain the transmission cycle of diarrhoeal pathogens.
